title: Being sangha
tomorrow: what do you do when the community you love starts a fight?

lines: ONE PERSON DOES THE BORING PART.
A HEAVY POT, LIFTED WITHOUT A WORD.
cards: Group projects have a pattern: one person does the boring part while everyone else does the fun part.
At the lunch after Sunday chanting at Ông's old temple, Mai noticed one auntie washing every dish alone while everyone else talked.
Long ago, the Buddha visited three monks living together in a park called Gosinga and asked how they were getting along. Anuruddha answered with a water pot.
Whoever comes back first from the alms round sets out the seats and the water. Whoever finds the water pot empty fills it.

teach.b: Ask Anuruddha how they live like that, and his answer is one question he asks himself: why don't I set aside what I want, and do what these friends want? They are different in body, he says, but one in mind.
The sutta pictures them blending like milk and water, looking at each other with kind eyes. Notice what being sangha means in that story. Not speeches about community.
Filling the pot when you find it empty. Signaling with a hand so nobody lifts alone. Setting out the seat before anyone asks.
At a temple today it looks the same. Someone cooks for the monks. Someone sweeps.
Someone comes early to unlock the door and light the incense. Someone sits beside an older person through the chanting so she isn't alone.
Buddhists count that as practice, not as chores around the practice: the community's path is kept walkable by a lot of quiet hands.
Being sangha is the second half of finding one.
And it doesn't require being asked. Mai can't fix the whole kitchen. She can pick up a towel.

how: Temple life depends on lay volunteers who cook for the monks, clean, open the hall, prepare offerings and help elders through ceremonies; Buddhists count this service to the community as part of practice.

o: showing up to keep other people's practice going
joining a temple board as an official member
living as a monk in a monastery for a season

games.q: life at Gosinga — tap the pairs.
p: sets out the seats and water
a wave of the hand, lifted together
why not set aside what I want?

s: the three monks at Gosinga talked every chore through together
they signaled with a hand and lifted the pot together, without a word.
Anuruddha said the three were different in body but one in mind
the sutta pictures them blending like milk and water.
being sangha mostly means attending the big ceremonies
in the story it's filling the pot and setting out the seats.

games.q: at your aunt's temple, the dinner after chanting runs late and the kitchen is a wreck. everyone's chatting and you're tired. what would Gosinga suggest?
o: take a towel beside whoever's washing; say little, lift together.
find whoever's in charge and propose a cleaning rota for next time.
leave it; the kitchen is the volunteers' practice, yours is chanting.
games.why: at Gosinga, whoever found the pot empty filled it, and two lifted what one couldn't, without a speech. the kitchen is part of the practice.

practice: Find one thing near you that's empty and meant to be full: a water glass, a pitcher, a bird feeder, a pet's bowl. Fill it slowly, for whoever uses it next, and listen to the sound it makes.
Then set it down and rest while the sit runs.

wordCard.voice: Being sangha: not only finding the community, but being one of the hands that keeps it going.

orig.note: Pali: in harmony, united; how the sutta describes the monks at Gosinga.

carryVoice: Here's the line: show up, because the pot gets filled by whoever finds it empty. Sixteen days in, and counting.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 31 (Culagosinga Sutta: the monks at Gosinga)
